Nāmdev
(A. D. 1270-1320)
------------------------------------------
The path to perfection as shown by the Hindu scriptures is twofold: the ज्ञानमार्ग (the path of knowledge) and the bhaktimārga (the path of devotion).
Out of these two, the latter is much easier to practise and hence more popular. In this regard, the contribution of the various saints of the भक्ति Movement, spread over a long period—7th to 18th century—is stupendous. They not only saved the Hindu society from the impact of the external forces of aggression but also helped it to achieve greater internal cohesion and unity.
The saints of Maharashtra, starting with Sant Jñāneśvar (or Jñānadev) (A. D. 1275-1296), held sway for over five hundred years in this field and revolutionised the life of the common people.
One such saint, a musician and composer of great repute, was नाम्देव् (also spelt as Nāmadeva), a contemporary of Sant Jñāneśvar himself.
Nāmdev was born on the Kārttika śuddha एकादशी day (eleventh day of the bright half of the month of Kārttika, known as Utthāna or Prabodhinī एकादशी, usually in November), a day considered as very sacred for the worship of the Lord विष्णु. His ड़थेर् was Dāmāśeṭ, a tailor by profession and Gonnāī Bāī was the मोथेर्.
Once, when नाम्देव् was a little boy, he was asked to take milk from his होउसे and offer it to Lord पाण्डुरङ्ग at the nearby temple. When he did so and found that the stone image was not drinking the milk, he became so remorseful that he decided to break his head against the stone pedestal. Moved by the child’s intense faith and devotion, the Lord appeared before him and actually drank the milk! Though the parents would not believe his version, they were wonder-struck to see it for themselves, the next day.
This experience made them give नाम्देव् full freedom to pursue the devotional path, of singing and praying.
In course of time नाम्देव् was married to Rājaībāī who proved to be a devoted wife and a great help in his spiritual pursuits.
Nāmdev started living in पण्ढर्पुर् itself, spending most of his time in singing the अभङ्गस् (Marāṭhī devotional songs) composed by him.
Once, all the contemporary saints and devotees of Lord पाण्डुरङ्ग assembled in the होउसे of Gorā Kumbhār (Gorā, the potter). Sant Jñāneśvar, their leader, jokingly asked Gorā to test whether the ‘pots’ that had assembled their, were ‘well-baked’ or not. When Gorā started the test, by gently stroking the heads of the saints who had gathered, with his pot-shaping stick, नाम्देव् protested against this rude method of testing, because of which, he was declared as the only unripe, unbaked, pot! However, on the advice of the Lord Himself, he got spiritual initiation from a qualified guru—Visobā Khecar —thereby completing his evolution into full sainthood.
While on a पिल्ग्रिमगे to various sacred places, he is said to have performed the miracle of the water of a deep well rising to the ground level and a temple of शिव turn in the direction of his group which was singing devotional songs at the back of the temple as per the orders of the priests.
Nāmdev has composed a large number of अभङ्गस् which are popular in Maharashtra even now. He has praised the path of devotion in preference to the path of knowledge. Eighty of these अभङ्गस् (in Hindi) have been included in the Ādigranth (Granth Sāhib), the sacred scripture of सिखिस्म्.

nambūdiri
------------------------------------------
This is the name of a dominant caste in the Kerala State.
The nambūdiris are orthodox brāh-maṇas, well-versed in the Vedic and the tāntrik lore. They were the chief land-owners before independence.
They followed a distinctive मर्रिअगे alliance (called ‘sambandham’) with the nāyars who are kṣattriyas and have adopted the matrilineal descent system.
The eldest son of a नम्बूदिरि married a नम्बूदिरि girl whereas the younger sons had a loose type of मर्रिअगे (‘sambandham’) for the sake of progeny, with nāyar girls. However, neither party to a sambandham union becomes a member of the other’s family. Consequently there is no legal responsibility or obligation on the part of the ‘husband’ towards the ‘wife’ or the children. The children belong to the ‘tarwad’ (joint family) descended from a common ancestress.
There are four subcastes among the nambūdiris, the ‘nambūdiripād’ being considered the highest.

nāmakaraṇa
(‘the act of naming [the baby]’)
------------------------------------------
Nāmakaraṇa or the ritualistic act of giving a name to a newborn baby is an important saṁskāra or sacrament in the life of a Hindu. Almost all sections of the Hindus, irrespective of their caste affiliations, have some sort of ritualistic or social pattern or method to be adopted in naming the baby.
During the Vedic age, the names of persons generally had two parts: the actual name and a patronymic or metronomic. For instance, in the name Kākṣīvanta Auśija (Pañcaviṁśa Brāhmaṇa 14.11.17), the first is the popular name and the second derived from the name of his मोथेर् Uśijā. And, in the name Vidagdha शाकल्य (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.1), the former is his name and the latter indicates that he was the son of Śakala.
Sometimes the name could reflect the place also as in Kauśāmbeya (resident of Kauśāmbi).
It is interesting to note that the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (6.4.24-28) describes the नामकरण ceremony to some extent.
Generally speaking, the नामकरण should be performed on a day after the tenth day of birth. It can be on the 11th, 12th or the 16th day.
As regards the composition, the name of a boy should consist of two or four or an even number of syllables while that of a girl must have an odd number. Also, the name must begin with a mṛdu letter (sonant) like ba, ga, da, and so on.
The names may be derived from that of a deity or a sage or an ancestor.
Though naming the girl-child after a river was prohibited in the earlier period, it is now quite common.
According to the धर्मशास्त्रस्, every child must be given a fourfold name according to the नक्षत्र (asterism) under which it is born, the deity of the month of birth, the family deity and a popular name, the last one being commonly used for all practical purposes.
Each of the 27 nakṣatras has four pādas (quarters) and certain letters of the alphabet are assigned to them. The child—male or female—born in that particular pāda must be assigned that name beginning with that letter. For instance, a baby born under अश्विनी 4th pāda must have a name beginning with ‘la’ (Lakṣmaṇa, Latā etc.).
As regards the deities ruling over the twelve months, all of them are aspects of विष्णु like कृष्ण, अनन्त, Hari, Upendra and so on. One of these is given depending upon the month. If a baby is born in the month of Mārgaśira (generally December) its special name is कृष्ण.
The third is the name associated with the family deity (kuladevatā), the words dāsa, datta or भक्त being added at the end. For example, if the family god is राम, the child’s name will be रामदास or Rāmadatta or Rāmabhakta.
The last is the popular name which is used throughout life. It should be easy to pronounce and sweet to hear. It should also signify fame or wealth or power which everyone naturally desires to possess.
It may be mentioned here, in passing, about the practice in some sections of the Hindu society, of giving awkward, disgusting or even repulsive names to their babies by the parents who have lost their previous issues, to frighten away evil spirits, diseases and death!
Some धर्मशास्त्रस् advocate the adding of the words śarma or deva, varma or trātā, bhūti or datta or gupta, and dāsa, at the end of the names given for the members of the four varṇas respectively.
A brief account of the नामकरण ceremony as given by the गृह्यसूत्रस् like those of शाङ्खायन (1.24.4), आश्वलायन (1.15.4) and Pāraskara (1.17) may now be given.
After the expiry of the jātāśaucha period (ceremonial impurity caused by the birth of the baby) (generally, after ten days of birth) the होउसे has to be washed and purified. The मोथेर् and the baby should be bathed. Then the मोथेर् gives the baby to the ड़थेर्. The ड़थेर् touches the breaths of the baby to awaken its चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. Then the name is given as follows. The ड़थेर् leaning towards the right ear of the babe addresses it thus: ‘O child! thou art the devotee of the kuladevatā...., so thy name is....; thou art born in such and such māsa or month, so thy name is....; thou art born under such and such नक्षत्र (constellation), so thy name is .....; and thy popular name is....’
The ब्राह्मणस् assembled there should say, ‘May the name be established!’
Then the ड़थेर् should make the baby salute the assembled ब्राह्मणस् who will bless it.
Afterwards, there will be a feast for all the ब्राह्मणस् and the relatives and friends.

namaskāra
(‘obeisance’)
------------------------------------------
Greeting one another, especially when one meets others for the first time in the day, is a common phenomenon of courtesy in all societies.
According to the Hindu religious and cultural traditions, as enshrined in the आगमस्, the धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस्, this greeting can assume several forms. ‘Namaskāra’ is the most common and general term used for such forms of showing respect or reverence.
Derived from the root-verb ‘nam,’ which means ‘to bend’, the word ‘namaskāra’ connotes bending before one’s superiors in humility, to show respect.
It may also mean ‘not mine’ (na = not; maḥ = mine), ‘but thine,’ reflecting an attitude of total surrender.
Several varieties of नमस्कार have been mentioned in the Hindu scriptural works, like अभिवादन, añjali and praṇāma.
In अभिवादन, a person (who should be a द्विज or belonging to the first three castes) keeps his hands covering the ears and recites his name along with other details concerning his गोत्र and प्रवर or lineage, the Veda to which he belongs, the sūtra work, the dictates of which are being followed in his family and so on. (See ABHIVĀDANA for details.)
In añjali, the two palms of the hand are joined in a mood of supplication.
Praṇāma is a special form of reverential salutation and prostration before the image of a deity in a temple, one’s गुरु (spiritual preceptor), a saṁnyāsin (monk), one’s parents and highly venerated persons.
This praṇāma can be ‘aṣṭāṅga’ (done with eight limbs viz, the two feet, the two knees, the two arms, the chest and the head touching the ground) or ‘pañcāṅga’ (done with five limbs, viz, the two knees, the two hands and the head touching the ground).
There is another method of नमस्कार wherein the person joins the palms of his hands and places them on his own head. This is resorted to when the salutation is casual and the object (or person) for whom it is meant, is not regarded as very holy.
Some of the पुराणस् extol the praṇāma properly done as equal to an अश्वमेध sacrifice!
The number of praṇāmas to be done in a temple may vary from 3 to 48.
Another aspect of reverence in a temple, connected with praṇāma, is प्रदक्षिण or circumambulation. It is going round the deity or the गर्भगृह (sanctum) keeping it always on the right. The number of such circumambulations to various deities is: one for चण्डी (Divine मोथेर्); seven for सूर्य (Sun-god); three for गणपति; four for विष्णु and three for शिव.
The form of circumambulation may be triangular (for देवी), crescent-like (for शिवलिङ्ग) and circular for other deities.
When praṇāma is done to elders or holy persons, they may bless the supplicant with such words as ‘svasti’ (= auspiciousness), ‘āyuṣmān bhava’ (‘May you live long!’) ‘vardhasva’ (‘May you be prosperous!’) and so on.
